primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Chediak-Higashi syndrome from biallelic LYST dysfunction causing abnormal lysosomal trafficking and giant cytoplasmic granules
mechanism: Loss of LYST function disrupts lysosomal and lysosome-related organelle trafficking and fission. Leukocytes develop giant azurophilic granules and impaired antimicrobial function; melanocytes show abnormal melanosome handling, producing partial oculocutaneous albinism.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent pyogenic skin and respiratory infections, easy bruising, photophobia, and silvery-gray hair. Examination shows partial oculocutaneous hypopigmentation. A peripheral blood smear shows very large azurophilic granules within neutrophils and monocytes.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this combination of findings?
distractor_notes: Chronic granulomatous disease causes defective phagocyte oxidative burst and recurrent catalase-positive infections but does not cause partial albinism with giant leukocyte granules.

Griscelli syndrome type 2 can cause pigment dilution and immune dysregulation, but it is associated with RAB27A dysfunction rather than the characteristic giant azurophilic leukocyte granules of LYST deficiency.
Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome causes oculocutaneous albinism and a platelet dense-granule defect but does not produce giant azurophilic granules in neutrophils.

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 causes recurrent bacterial infections, impaired pus formation, delayed umbilical cord separation, and neutrophilia due to CD18 deficiency, not pigment dilution with giant lysosomal granules.
key_expl: Partial oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent pyogenic infection, bleeding tendency, and giant azurophilic granules in granulocytes strongly indicate Chediak-Higashi syndrome. It is caused by biallelic LYST variants that disrupt lysosomal trafficking and lysosome-related organelle biology.
objective: Recognize Chediak-Higashi syndrome from the combination of partial albinism, recurrent infections, bleeding tendency, and giant cytoplasmic granules in leukocytes, and connect the phenotype to LYST-dependent lysosomal trafficking.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Carotid sinus stretch is conveyed to the nucleus tractus solitarius through glossopharyngeal afferent fibers
mechanism: Increased arterial pressure stretches carotid sinus baroreceptors and increases afferent firing through the sinus nerve of Hering, a branch of cranial nerve IX, to the nucleus tractus solitarius. Central integration then decreases sympathetic output and increases vagal efferent activity, lowering heart rate and vascular tone.
vignette: During a physiology study, brief external pressure is applied over the carotid sinus of a healthy volunteer. Heart rate and arterial pressure fall transiently. In a second trial, a local nerve block selectively abolishes sensory transmission from the carotid sinus while leaving vagal efferent function intact; the hemodynamic response disappears.
lead: The blocked afferent fibers travel primarily in which cranial nerve?
distractor_notes: The facial nerve carries branchial motor, taste, and parasympathetic functions but is not the principal carotid sinus baroreceptor afferent pathway.
The vagus nerve carries aortic arch baroreceptor afferents and cardiac parasympathetic efferents, but carotid sinus afferents travel mainly through cranial nerve IX.
The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius motor function and does not carry carotid sinus baroreceptor afferents.
The hypoglossal nerve provides motor innervation to the tongue and does not mediate the carotid baroreflex.
key_expl: Carotid sinus mechanoreceptor afferents pass through the sinus nerve of Hering into the glossopharyngeal nerve and terminate in the nucleus tractus solitarius. Aortic arch baroreceptor afferents instead travel through the vagus nerve.
objective: Distinguish the glossopharyngeal afferent limb of the carotid sinus baroreflex from the vagal afferent limb of the aortic arch reflex and the vagal efferent response to the heart.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Conjugated bile acids are reclaimed from the terminal ileum by apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter SLC10A2
mechanism: Most conjugated bile acids are actively reclaimed at the apical membrane of terminal ileal enterocytes by the sodium-dependent bile acid transporter ASBT (SLC10A2). They then exit across the basolateral membrane through OSTalpha/beta and return to the liver through portal blood.
vignette: A 39-year-old man with Crohn disease undergoes resection of the terminal ileum. Several months later, he has increased fecal bile acid loss and a reduced circulating bile acid pool despite preserved hepatic bile synthesis.
lead: Loss of which normal epithelial transport process most directly explains these findings?
correct: Apical sodium-dependent uptake of bile acids into terminal ileal enterocytes by ASBT
distractors: Basolateral export of bile acids from ileal enterocytes by OSTalpha/beta
Basolateral uptake of portal bile acids into hepatocytes by NTCP
Canalicular secretion of bile acids from hepatocytes by BSEP
Apical chloride secretion by CFTR in cholangiocytes
distractor_notes: OSTalpha/beta mediates basolateral exit of bile acids from ileal enterocytes after apical uptake; the resected terminal ileum primarily removes the ASBT uptake step.
NTCP is located on the sinusoidal/basolateral surface of hepatocytes and reclaims bile acids from portal blood rather than from the intestinal lumen.
BSEP exports bile acids from hepatocytes into bile canaliculi and is not the transporter responsible for intestinal reclamation.
CFTR contributes to chloride and bicarbonate handling in cholangiocytes but does not mediate enterohepatic reclamation of bile acids.
key_expl: The terminal ileum is the major site of active conjugated bile acid reclamation. ASBT/SLC10A2 transports luminal bile acids across the apical membrane of ileal enterocytes; terminal ileal resection therefore increases fecal bile acid loss and shrinks the enterohepatic bile acid pool.
objective: Localize the major active bile acid-reabsorption step to apical ASBT in terminal ileal enterocytes and distinguish it from OSTalpha/beta, NTCP, and BSEP transport steps elsewhere in the enterohepatic circuit.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia due to reduced calcium-sensing receptor signaling
mechanism: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in CASR most commonly raise the calcium set point for suppressing PTH and increase renal tubular calcium reabsorption. Patients therefore have lifelong mild hypercalcemia, inappropriately normal or mildly elevated PTH, and relative hypocalciuria.
vignette: A 28-year-old woman is found incidentally to have a serum calcium concentration of 11.0 mg/dL. She feels well. Serum parathyroid hormone is at the upper end of the reference range, renal function is normal, and the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio is 0.006. Her mother has had mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia for many years.
distractors: Primary hyperparathyroidism due to a parathyroid adenoma
Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease
distractor_notes: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy usually suppresses endogenous PTH and does not produce lifelong familial hypocalciuria.

Primary hyperparathyroidism can produce hypercalcemia with nonsuppressed PTH, but urinary calcium excretion is generally not as low as the characteristic calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 seen in FHH.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease usually occurs with reduced kidney function and often low or normal calcium rather than mild familial hypercalcemia.
Vitamin D intoxication suppresses PTH and generally increases intestinal calcium absorption and urinary calcium excretion rather than causing marked relative hypocalciuria.
key_expl: Mild lifelong hypercalcemia, a nonsuppressed PTH concentration, a first-degree relative with the same phenotype, and a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 strongly support familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Most cases result from heterozygous loss-of-function CASR variants.
objective: Differentiate familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism by recognizing the combination of familial mild hypercalcemia, nonsuppressed PTH, and marked relative hypocalciuria.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Acetazolamide inhibits proximal tubular carbonic anhydrase and causes bicarbonaturia with metabolic acidosis
mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase facilitates proximal tubular bicarbonate reclamation by enabling conversion between carbon dioxide, water, carbonic acid, bicarbonate, and hydrogen ions. Acetazolamide inhibits this process, reducing sodium bicarbonate reabsorption and increasing urinary bicarbonate loss, which lowers serum bicarbonate.
vignette: A 31-year-old climber begins acetazolamide before a rapid ascent to high altitude. After several doses, serum bicarbonate is lower than baseline and urinary bicarbonate excretion is increased.
lead: Which nephron effect most directly accounts for this acid-base change?
correct: Reduced proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption due to carbonic anhydrase inhibition
distractors: Reduced sodium-potassium-2 chloride cotransport in the thick ascending limb
Reduced sodium-chloride cotransport in the distal convoluted tubule
Reduced epithelial sodium channel activity in principal cells
Reduced mineralocorticoid receptor activation in collecting-duct principal cells
distractor_notes: Inhibition of NKCC2 is the mechanism of loop diuretics and does not directly explain acetazolamide-induced bicarbonaturia.
Inhibition of the distal convoluted tubule sodium-chloride cotransporter is the mechanism of thiazide diuretics, not carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
ENaC inhibition is produced by potassium-sparing agents such as amiloride and is not the primary proximal tubular action of acetazolamide.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism occurs with spironolactone or eplerenone and does not cause the characteristic proximal bicarbonate loss of acetazolamide.
key_expl: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, decreasing bicarbonate reclamation. The resulting bicarbonaturia lowers serum bicarbonate and produces a metabolic acidosis that helps stimulate ventilation at altitude.
objective: Connect acetazolamide therapy to proximal tubular carbonic anhydrase inhibition, bicarbonaturia, and reduced serum bicarbonate, and distinguish this mechanism from other diuretic targets.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Weber syndrome results from a ventral midbrain lesion affecting ipsilateral oculomotor fascicles and the cerebral peduncle
mechanism: A ventral midbrain lesion can injure exiting oculomotor nerve fascicles together with descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the cerebral peduncle. This produces an ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral weakness.
vignette: A 68-year-old man suddenly develops left-sided ptosis. The left eye rests down and out and the left pupil is dilated. Strength is markedly reduced in the right arm and leg, but sensation is intact and there is no prominent tremor or limb ataxia.
lead: Which pair of structures is most likely injured by the same lesion?
correct: Left oculomotor fascicles and left cerebral peduncle
distractors: Left oculomotor fascicles and left red nucleus
Left trochlear fascicles and left superior cerebellar peduncle
Left abducens fascicles and left corticospinal tract in the ventral pons
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus and left medial lemniscus
distractor_notes: Involvement of the red nucleus with oculomotor fascicles is associated with contralateral tremor or ataxia rather than the predominantly pyramidal weakness described.
Trochlear and superior cerebellar peduncle lesions do not produce the classic ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.
A ventral pontine lesion involving the abducens fascicles and corticospinal tract would cause an ipsilateral sixth-nerve deficit rather than the third-nerve findings in the vignette.
A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and medial lemniscus injury would affect contralateral vibration/proprioception rather than produce this pattern.
key_expl: Ipsilateral complete oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis localizes to the ventral midbrain. The lesion involves CN III fascicles and descending corticospinal/corticobulbar fibers in the cerebral peduncle, the classic anatomic substrate of Weber syndrome.
objective: Localize a ventral midbrain lesion by pairing ipsilateral oculomotor fascicle injury with contralateral pyramidal weakness from cerebral-peduncle involvement.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency causes osteopetrosis by impairing osteoclast acidification of the resorption lacuna
mechanism: Osteoclasts require intracellular carbonic anhydrase II to generate hydrogen ions from carbon dioxide and water. Protons are pumped across the ruffled border to acidify the resorption lacuna and dissolve hydroxyapatite. CA2 deficiency therefore impairs bone resorption and can also cause renal tubular acidosis and intracranial calcifications.
vignette: A 9-year-old boy has recurrent fractures despite diffusely increased bone density on radiographs. Laboratory testing shows a chronic hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Head imaging shows intracranial calcifications. Genetic testing identifies a pathogenic variant in CA2.
lead: Which osteoclast function is most directly impaired?
correct: Generation of hydrogen ions needed to acidify the bone-resorption lacuna
distractors: Binding of RANKL to RANK during osteoclast differentiation
Secretion of type I collagen by osteoblasts
Release of alkaline phosphatase into osteoid by osteoblasts
Synthesis of osteoprotegerin by stromal cells
distractor_notes: RANKL-RANK signaling controls osteoclast differentiation, but a CA2 defect specifically impairs acid generation in mature osteoclasts.
Type I collagen is produced mainly by osteoblasts and forms osteoid; its synthesis is not the primary defect in carbonic anhydrase II osteopetrosis.
Alkaline phosphatase supports mineralization by osteoblasts and does not explain failure of osteoclast-mediated resorption in CA2 deficiency.
Osteoprotegerin is a soluble RANKL decoy receptor that regulates osteoclastogenesis but is not the protein encoded by CA2.
key_expl: Carbonic anhydrase II provides hydrogen ions that osteoclasts pump into the resorption lacuna. Loss of CA2 reduces acidification, preventing normal mineral dissolution and bone resorption; the same enzyme defect can produce renal tubular acidosis and intracranial calcifications.
objective: Explain the osteopetrosis–renal tubular acidosis phenotype of carbonic anhydrase II deficiency by linking CA2 to osteoclast proton generation and acidification of the resorption compartment.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency blocks conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
mechanism: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is a mitochondrial enzyme that uses adenosylcobalamin, a vitamin B12-derived cofactor, to isomerize methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA during propionyl-CoA metabolism. Deficiency causes methylmalonic acid accumulation and episodes of high-anion-gap metabolic decompensation.
vignette: A 3-month-old infant develops vomiting, lethargy, tachypnea, and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis after protein feeding. Urine organic acid analysis shows markedly increased methylmalonic acid without homocystinuria. Cellular studies show normal uptake and formation of adenosylcobalamin.
lead: Which metabolic conversion is most directly impaired?
distractors: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacids to their acyl-CoA derivatives
distractor_notes: Homocysteine-to-methionine conversion requires methionine synthase and methylcobalamin; isolated methylmalonic acidemia without homocystinuria points away from this pathway.
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA and requires biotin; deficiency causes propionic acidemia rather than an isolated block at methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and is unrelated to the characteristic methylmalonic acid accumulation.
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease and does not selectively block methylmalonyl-CoA conversion.
key_expl: Normal adenosylcobalamin synthesis with isolated methylmalonic acid accumulation points to the mutase itself. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase directly converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix.
objective: Identify the metabolic reaction catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and distinguish isolated mutase deficiency from defects of propionyl-CoA carboxylase and cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Patent urachus from persistence of the allantoic connection between bladder dome and umbilicus
mechanism: The urachus derives from the intraembryonic allantoic connection between the developing bladder and umbilicus and normally obliterates. Complete persistence creates a patent tract that can drain urine from the umbilicus.
vignette: A term newborn has persistent clear fluid leaking from the umbilicus. The drainage increases during urination. Ultrasound shows a continuous tubular tract extending from the dome of the urinary bladder to the umbilicus.
lead: Which congenital anomaly is most likely?
distractor_notes: An omphalomesenteric fistula connects ileum to the umbilicus and may drain enteric contents rather than urine from a tract continuous with the bladder.
A urachal cyst retains a closed central segment and does not create a complete bladder-to-umbilicus channel for urine drainage.
An umbilical-urachal sinus is open at the umbilical end but closed toward the bladder, so it does not produce urine leakage that increases with voiding.
A vesicourachal diverticulum remains open toward the bladder but closed at the umbilical end and therefore does not drain through the umbilicus.
key_expl: Urine leaking from the umbilicus and imaging of a continuous tract from the bladder dome to the umbilicus are diagnostic of a patent urachus, caused by persistence of the allantoic/urachal lumen.
objective: Differentiate a patent urachus from other urachal remnants and an omphalomesenteric fistula by recognizing urine drainage through a complete bladder-to-umbilicus tract.
clues: tract from bladder dome to umbilicus

diagnosis: Partial verification bias occurs when receipt of the reference standard depends on index-test results
mechanism: Diagnostic-accuracy estimates are biased when only a selected subset of participants receives the definitive reference standard, particularly when verification is more likely after a positive index test. This is partial verification, also called work-up bias.
vignette: Investigators evaluate a new noninvasive test for pancreatic cancer in 1,200 adults. All participants receive the new test. Because the definitive reference procedure is invasive, nearly every participant with a positive new test undergoes the reference procedure, whereas only a small fraction of participants with a negative new test undergo it. Sensitivity and specificity are then calculated only among participants whose disease status was verified.
lead: Which source of bias is introduced by this study design?
distractor_notes: Incorporation bias occurs when the index test itself is included in or contributes to the reference standard used to define disease status; that is not described here.
Observer bias reflects systematic differences in measurement or interpretation by observers and is not the principal problem created by selective use of the reference standard.
Recall bias arises from differential accuracy of remembered prior exposures and is not relevant to this prospective diagnostic-test verification process.

Spectrum bias occurs when the study population does not represent the full clinical spectrum in which the test will be used; the defining defect here is selective reference-standard verification based on the index result.
key_expl: Only a selected subset of patients receives the reference standard, and selection is strongly related to the index-test result. This is partial verification or work-up bias and can distort estimated sensitivity and specificity.
objective: Recognize partial verification bias in diagnostic-accuracy studies when definitive disease verification is preferentially performed in participants with particular index-test results.
clues: accuracy calculated only among verified participants
